title: Headroom deficit rapid response and autoscale hardening
creator: Ava Morales
description: Summary: During a morning traffic surge we observed the dedicated GPU pool report significantly reduced available headroom for several minutes, triggering throttling and customer impact for a subset of Dedicated customers. This ticket captures the emergency triage steps taken, the technical root cause analysis, temporary mitigations, and a prioritized set of permanent hardening tasks for autoscaling and fleet controls.
timeline: 2026-03-09 09:12 UTC: SLO alert - p95 latency for dedicated-route 'gen-heavy' crossed 2s. Automated pager notified on-call.
2026-03-09 09:15 UTC: On-call assembled. Observed sustained enqueue growth and reduced free GPU slots reported by fleet manager UI.
2026-03-09 09:20 UTC: Emergency traffic triage - routed low-priority burst traffic to hosted pool and disabled scheduled batch jobs for the cluster.
2026-03-09 09:28 UTC: Temporary reserve capacity created by spinning up 3 reserved instances from spare pool (manual override). Latency improved after 90s.
2026-03-09 09:45 UTC: Hotfix deployed to autoscaler to extend scaling cooldown from 30s to 120s to avoid flapping; immediate side-effects monitored.
2026-03-09 10:30 UTC: Service recovered to normal; customers notified via status page and follow-up comms drafted.
2026-03-10 11:00 UTC: Post-incident triage meeting; assigned investigation owners and drafted this runbook and action list.
runbook_steps: 1) Detect: Validate alerts against both fleet free_slots metric and realtime enqueue depth to reduce false positives.
2) Contain: Shift non-critical traffic to hosted pool routing policy and disable low-priority scheduled workloads in affected region.
3) Stabilize: Manually provision reserved capacity from spare pools (safest short-term) and increase autoscale cooldown to stop thrash.
4) Observe: Verify KV cache hit rates and kernel queue lengths to ensure new capacity addresses backlog, not a systemic processing issue.
5) Restore: Roll forward permanent fixes after validation in canary; document timeline for customer comms and RCA.
6) Close: Capture lessons learned, close out action items, and schedule DR drill for headroom deficits.
mitigation_actions_taken: Manually provisioned 3 reserved nodes from the spare pool (region us-west2) to create >30% headroom within 3 minutes.
Routed burst-priority traffic to hosted API endpoints via routing policy 'burst-to-hosted' to limit Dedicated exposure.
Deployed temporary autoscaler throttle patch (COOLDOWN=120s) to reduce rapid scale-up/scale-down cycles.
Rolled back a recent runtime kernel scheduler tweak (PR #4523) that increased per-worker CPU contention under short high-concurrency bursts.
Notified affected customers on status.redwood.ai and opened support tickets for high-impact tenants.
root_cause_summary: Primary root cause was an interaction between a recent runtime scheduler change and conservative autoscaler thresholds. The scheduler tweak increased transient CPU contention for small batches, causing node heartbeats to queue and the fleet manager to mark slots as temporarily unavailable. The autoscaler interpreted the short spike in reported unavailable slots as a capacity drop and began aggressive resizes which then thrashed due to short-lived signals. Contributing factors: lack of a short-duration smoothing window on the free_slots metric and missing integration test for kernel changes against synthetic burst traffic.
postmortem_conclusions: Metric smoothing: Add a short 'burst window' (30s moving median) for free_slots and enqueue_depth so autoscaler decisions ignore micro-bursts.
Autoscaler logic: Guard against scale actions when CPU-based health indicators show transient scheduling contention; prefer adding reserve nodes instead of immediate aggressive scale-up.
Release gating: Require a synthetic burst test in CI for runtime scheduler patches that simulates high-concurrency 10s-60s bursts.
Runbook updates: Add explicit traffic diversion steps and a quick-reserve procedure for the on-call runbook page.
